title: Humanity and agency in the world’s conflict zones
text:
Humanity and agency in the world’s conflict zones
In our story from northern Nigeria this week, we show how individuals living in times of crisis continue to demonstrate dignity, agency, and hope.
More than a decade ago, armed militants abducted nearly 300 teenage girls from their secondary school in northeastern Nigeria. This act of violence, perpetrated by the Islamist extremist group Boko Haram, prompted international outrage.
Michelle Obama spoke out about the incident; so did celebrities from Anne Hathaway to Mary J. Blige. The #BringBackOurGirls label trended on social media and prompted rallies. And for a moment, the world seemed focused on an African conflict that involved religious and ethnic divisions, economic and natural resources, and a rapidly expanding humanitarian toll.
But then, the world seemed to lose interest.
The fighting, though, has continued in northern Nigeria. Boko Haram has kidnapped other schoolgirls. And the Trump administration has condemned what it describes as the religious persecution of Christians in northern Nigeria and last year sent military and intelligence support to the region. Still, the conflict has become one of dozens around the world that rarely make global headlines.
In this issue, we bring attention back to the situation in northern Nigeria, which the United Nations says has displaced millions of people and has contributed to widespread hunger in the region.
Nigerian officials there have declared – not for the first time – that the worst of the conflict is over. But as contributor Ogar Monday finds, many families are still searching for loved ones.
This is not an easy story, but it is also not without hope. The people Ogar interviewed exude dignity, action, and agency. They are joining with their neighbors to take action – and to bring families back together.
Finding people at the center of a crisis and sharing their full humanity is a hallmark of Monitor journalism, says Africa editor Ryan Lenora Brown.
“It is important to not just frame people as victims of terrible circumstances,” she says. “We are always trying to show people as complete humans.”
